title: The Day the Robots Went on Strike
summary: A curious girl visiting a toy factory helps the engineers trace a strange software update to one small coding bug that made all the helper robots freeze.
poll: Machines can misbehave, but they can never truly choose to disobey like a person can.

versions.title: The Day the Robots Went on Strike
versions.text:
Dalia visits a factory. Robots work there. They sort toys. They pack boxes.

Last night, the robots got an update. An update is new code. It should make them work well.

This morning, something is wrong. They will not work right. One robot says one word again and again. Another robot picks up a toy. Then it puts the toy back down. It will not pack the box.

"The robots are on strike!" says a worker. He is just joking. They do not get mad. They do what the code says.

Ms. Huda looks at the code. Dalia looks too. She looks very close at the screen.

"Look!" says Dalia. "These two words are stuck!" The two words have no space. They can not read it. So they just stop.

Ms. Huda fixes the bug. She adds the space. They work again. They sort and pack like before.

The team claps for Dalia. She helped fix the whole place!

versions.title: The Day the Robots Went on Strike
versions.text:
Dalia is visiting the toy factory where her uncle works. Robots work there every day. They sort toys and pack them into boxes.

Last night, workers gave the robots a new update. An update is new code for a robot to follow. It should make the robots work better than before.

This morning, something is wrong. The robots will not work the way they should. One robot says the same word again and again. Another robot picks up a toy, then puts it right back down. It will not pack the toy into its box.

"Looks like the robots are on strike!" jokes one worker. He is just joking, of course. Robots can not really get mad and stop working. They can only do what their code tells them.

Ms. Huda is the lead worker at the factory. She sits down to study the new code. Dalia and her uncle watch closely. Dalia leans in and looks hard at the screen.

"Look right there!" says Dalia, pointing at the screen. "These two words are stuck together, with no space!" Two commands got joined into one word. The robots can not read a word like that, so they just freeze.

Ms. Huda fixes the tiny bug by typing in the missing space. One by one, the robots turn back on and sort and pack again, just like before.

The whole team claps and cheers for Dalia. Her sharp eyes helped fix the whole factory in a few minutes!

versions.title: The Day the Robots Went on Strike
versions.text:
Dalia is visiting the toy factory where her uncle works. Robots work there every day. They sort toys and pack them into boxes for shipping.

Last night, workers put a new update on every robot in the factory. An update is a new set of code for a robot to follow. It should make the robots work faster and better.

This morning, something is clearly wrong. The robots will not work the way they should. One robot keeps saying the same word, over and over. Another robot picks up a toy, then puts it right back down instead of packing it.

"Looks like the robots are on strike!" jokes one worker, laughing a little. Of course, robots can not really get angry and stop working on purpose. They can only follow what their code tells them.

Ms. Huda, the lead worker, sits down to study the new update, line by line. Dalia and her uncle gather around to watch. Dalia leans in and studies the screen with great interest.

"Look right there!" says Dalia, pointing at the screen. "Those two words are stuck together, with no space!" Two commands got joined into one strange word. The robots can not understand a word like that, so they just freeze in place.

Ms. Huda quickly fixes the tiny bug by typing in the missing space. One by one, the robots turn back on and sort and pack again, just like before.

The whole factory claps and cheers for Dalia. Her sharp eyes helped fix the whole factory in just a few minutes!

versions.title: The Day the Robots Went on Strike
versions.text:
Dalia is spending the day at the toy factory where her uncle, an engineer, works. Robots work there every day. They sort toys and pack them into boxes before the boxes are shipped out.

Last night, the factory's workers installed a new software update on every robot. An update is a new set of code for a robot to follow. It replaces the older instructions the robot used before.

But this morning, something is clearly wrong. The robots will not work the way they are supposed to. One robot keeps repeating the same word, over and over, without ever stopping. Another robot picks up a toy, then puts it right back down, instead of packing it into its box.

"Looks like the robots are on strike!" jokes one of the workers, laughing at the strange sight. Of course, robots can not really get angry and refuse to work on purpose. A robot can only follow whatever command its code gives it.

Ms. Huda, the factory's lead engineer, sits down to study the new update, line by line. Dalia and her uncle gather around to watch. Dalia leans in and studies the screen with real curiosity.

"Look right there!" Dalia suddenly says, pointing at one line on the screen. "Those two words are stuck together, with no space between them!" Two separate commands have joined into one confusing word. The robots can not understand a jumbled command like that, so they just freeze in place.

Ms. Huda quickly fixes the tiny bug. She types in the missing space between the two commands. One by one, the robots power back on and begin sorting and packing again, just as before.

Everyone in the factory claps and cheers for Dalia. Her sharp eyes helped fix the whole factory in just a few minutes.

versions.title: The Day the Robots Went on Strike
versions.text:
Dalia is spending the day at the toy factory where her uncle, an engineer, is employed, and dozens of helper robots labor there every single day, sorting toys and packing them neatly into boxes before those boxes are shipped off to stores scattered across the country.

Last night, the factory's technicians installed a brand-new software update onto every robot in the building, a revised set of code intended to replace the older instructions the robots had relied upon previously, correcting minor malfunctions that had lingered since the preceding version.

This morning, however, something is unmistakably wrong throughout the entire factory floor: the robots refuse to behave the way they are supposed to. One robot keeps repeating the exact same word, over and over, without ever pausing, while another picks up a toy and sets it right back down instead of packing it, as though it has simply forgotten which command comes next.

"Looks like the robots are on strike!" jokes one of the technicians, laughing nervously at the bizarre scene. Naturally, a robot cannot genuinely feel anger and refuse to work out of spite the way a person might, since it can only execute whatever command its underlying code provides, however strange that command might be.

Ms. Huda, the factory's lead engineer, sits down calmly to diagnose the malfunction, examining the new update line by line in search of anything irregular within its syntax. Dalia and her uncle gather around to observe, while Dalia studies the glowing screen with intense curiosity, determined to locate the problem herself.

"Look right there!" Dalia suddenly exclaims, pointing at one line of the algorithm. "Those two words are stuck together, with no space between them at all!" Two separate commands have merged into one unreadable word because of a tiny syntax error, and the robots cannot interpret a jumbled command of that sort, so each one simply freezes in place.

Ms. Huda swiftly corrects the bug by typing the missing space between the two commands, effectively overriding the flawed instruction with a working one. One by one, the robots power back on and resume sorting and packing exactly as before.

Everyone throughout the factory claps and cheers enthusiastically for Dalia, astonished that her remarkably sharp eyes helped repair the entire factory in mere minutes.

keyWords.definition: a machine that can be told what to do and can move or work on its own
keyWords.example: The robot moved across the floor to pick up the box.

keyWords.definition: new code or information added to a machine to change how it works
keyWords.example: The phone needed an update before it would work right.

keyWords.definition: a small mistake in computer code that makes something go wrong
keyWords.example: A tiny bug in the game made the character fall through the floor.

keyWords.definition: to do something useful for someone else
keyWords.example: She helped her little brother tie his shoes.

keyWords.definition: not able to move or change
keyWords.example: The toy car was stuck under the couch.

questions.stem: What is this story mostly about?
options: A girl who helps find a bug that made robots freeze
A girl who builds a brand-new toy factory from scratch
A girl who teaches all the robots how to talk
A girl who paints colorful boxes for toys
questions.why: The story is about Dalia helping find the small bug that made the factory's robots freeze.

wrong.B: Dalia visits a factory that already exists; she does not build one.
wrong.C: The story is not about teaching robots to talk.
wrong.D: The story does not mention painting boxes.

questions.stem: What happened to the robots the night before?
options: They ran out of power
They sorted extra toys
They got a new update
They went outside
questions.why: In the story, workers installed a new update on the robots the night before.

wrong.A: Running out of power is not mentioned.
wrong.B: Extra sorting is not mentioned as happening that night.
wrong.D: The robots do not go outside in the story.

questions.stem: Why do the robots freeze instead of working?
options: Two words in the code are stuck together with no space
The robots are too heavy for anyone to move
A worker quietly turned off every robot in the room
The robots are out of toys left to pack
questions.why: Dalia finds that two commands joined into one word the robots cannot read, so they freeze.

wrong.B: Weight is not the problem in the story.
wrong.C: No worker turns the robots off.
wrong.D: The robots still have toys; the bug is the problem.

questions.stem: Who notices the bug on the screen?
options: Ms. Huda
Eng. Yusuf
A worker
Dalia
questions.why: Dalia is the one who spots that two words are stuck together on the screen.

wrong.A: Ms. Huda fixes the bug after Dalia spots it.
wrong.B: Eng. Yusuf watches but does not spot the bug first.
wrong.C: The worker only jokes about the robots; he does not find the bug.

questions.stem: What does Ms. Huda do to fix the problem?
options: She buys several brand-new robots instead of the old ones
She adds the missing space between the two words
She unplugs the entire factory for the rest of the day
She asks all the robots to simply try again later
questions.why: Ms. Huda fixes the tiny bug by typing in the missing space.

wrong.A: The same robots work fine after the fix.
wrong.C: The story does not mention unplugging the factory.
wrong.D: Asking the robots to try again is not how the bug is fixed.

questions.stem: Why does a worker joke that the robots are "on strike"?
options: Because the robots look like they are refusing to work
Because the robots are asking for more pay
Because the robots are tired from working all day in the factory
Because the robots do not like their new update
questions.why: The robots freezing and refusing simple commands looks like they are refusing to work, which is why the worker jokes this way.

wrong.B: Robots do not ask for pay.
wrong.C: Tiredness is not a real reason, since robots do not get tired.
wrong.D: Robots do not actually like or dislike anything; the joke is just a joke.

questions.stem: What can you tell about robots from this story?
options: Robots only do exactly what their code tells them to do
Robots can choose to be angry and stop working
Robots understand jokes just like people really do
Robots are able to fix all of their own bugs
questions.why: The story explains that robots cannot really get angry; they just follow their code exactly.

wrong.B: The story says robots cannot really choose to get angry.
wrong.C: The story does not say robots understand jokes.
wrong.D: A person, Ms. Huda, fixes the bug, not the robots themselves.

questions.stem: Why does the author have Dalia, a visiting kid, find the bug instead of an adult?
options: To show that careful eyes can spot small mistakes, no matter who is looking
To show that children know more about machines than grown adults do in the factory
To explain in detail how big toy factories are usually built
To describe exactly what Dalia had for breakfast that morning
questions.why: Having a visiting kid spot the simple, easy-to-overlook mistake shows that a careful look can catch problems anyone might miss.

wrong.B: The story does not claim children generally know more than adults about machines.
wrong.C: The story does not explain factory construction.
wrong.D: The story never mentions breakfast.

LOW.prompt: Have you ever noticed a small mistake that others missed? Write about it, or imagine how you would feel if you were Dalia spotting the bug.
checklist: I clearly described a mistake and how it was noticed.
I used at least two details from the story.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
LOW.modelAnswer: If I were Dalia, I would feel excited and a little proud when I noticed the two stuck-together words on the screen. I would look closely at the update, just like Dalia did, to see what was different from before. When Ms. Huda used my idea to fix the bug and the robots started working again, I would feel very happy that my careful eyes helped the whole factory.

keyWords.example: The engineer checked each robot before it went back to work.

keyWords.definition: the programs and code that make a computer or robot run
keyWords.example: New software can change how a machine behaves without changing its parts.

keyWords.definition: to make someone or something unable to understand clearly
keyWords.example: The mixed-up instructions confused the new student.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the story?
options: A factory decides to stop using every single robot after they misbehave in one week
A visiting girl helps engineers trace a strange robot problem to one small coding bug
A factory builds a brand-new kind of helper robot from scratch with no help from anyone
An engineer argues loudly with a worker about the brand-new update to the factory system
questions.why: The story follows Dalia helping Ms. Huda and Eng. Yusuf find the bug that caused the strange robot behavior.

wrong.A: The factory keeps its robots and fixes the bug instead of giving them up.
wrong.C: No new robot is built in the story.
wrong.D: No argument between an engineer and a worker occurs.

questions.stem: What happened to the robots just before this morning's trouble began?
options: They were given a new software update
They were moved to a new building
They ran out of toys to sort
They were taken apart for cleaning
questions.why: The story says the factory's workers installed a new software update the night before.

wrong.B: Moving buildings is not mentioned.
wrong.C: Running out of toys is not the cause described.
wrong.D: Taking the robots apart is not mentioned.

questions.stem: What two strange behaviors do the robots show?
options: One sings a happy song; another dances around in circles for the crowd
One turns off completely; another suddenly catches on fire in the hall
One leaves the factory; another calls loudly for help from the street
One repeats a word; another puts a toy back down instead of packing it
questions.why: The story describes one robot repeating a word and another setting a toy back down instead of packing it.

wrong.A: Singing and dancing are not described in the story.
wrong.B: Neither robot turns off completely nor catches fire.
wrong.C: No robot leaves the factory or calls for help.

questions.stem: Why does the engineer's joke about a "strike" turn out not to be literally true?
options: The robots were actually asking for a well-deserved day off from their work
The robots were simply far too tired to keep on working all day long
Robots cannot feel anger and choose to stop working; they only follow their code
The robots were protesting the brand-new update on purpose, to show anger
questions.why: The story explains that robots cannot really get angry and refuse to work; they just follow what their code tells them.

wrong.A: Robots do not ask for time off.
wrong.B: Robots do not get tired the way people do.
wrong.D: A protest requires choosing to act, which robots cannot do.

questions.stem: In the story, the word confuse is best understood to mean —
options: to make something unable to understand clearly
to repair a broken machine part completely
to turn off a piece of factory software
to pack a box neatly and carefully
questions.why: The merged command confuses the robots because they cannot understand what it means.

wrong.B: Repairing a part is not what confuse means.
wrong.C: Turning off software is a separate idea.
wrong.D: Packing a box is unrelated to the meaning of confuse.

questions.stem: What can you infer caused the two commands to become one unreadable word?
options: A worker accidentally unplugging a robot overnight in the factory
A robot's motor overheating badly during the night
The toys being packed in the wrong order entirely
A missing space between two commands in the update's code
questions.why: Dalia notices that the two words are stuck together with no space, which is why the robots cannot read the command.

wrong.A: Unplugging a robot overnight is not mentioned in the story.
wrong.B: Motor overheating is not mentioned as a cause.
wrong.C: Toy order is unrelated to the frozen robots.

questions.stem: How is the robot problem in the story mainly solved?
options: By replacing every single robot in the factory with new ones
By adding the missing space between the two commands
By turning off the new update
By asking the robots to repeat the broken command
questions.why: Ms. Huda fixes the bug by typing in the missing space between the two merged commands.

wrong.A: The factory keeps using the same robots after the fix.
wrong.C: The update stays; only the small bug inside it is fixed.
wrong.D: Asking the robots to repeat a broken command would not fix it.

questions.stem: Why does the author include Dalia, a child, as the one who spots the bug?
options: To show that a fresh, careful look can catch a mistake experienced adults might overlook
To prove that children should run the entire factory instead of engineers, who are too slow
To explain why toy factories usually hire many extra young workers in the summer
To describe exactly how Dalia first learned to read code in school, step by step
questions.why: Dalia's fresh perspective helps her notice the small, easy-to-miss mistake that the engineers had not yet spotted.

wrong.B: The story does not suggest children should run the factory.
wrong.C: The story is not about hiring practices.
wrong.D: The story does not explain how Dalia learned to read code.

MID.prompt: Explain the problem the factory faced and how Dalia and Ms. Huda solved it. Use at least two details from the story.
checklist: I explained how it was solved, using at least two details.
I organized my ideas in a clear order.
MID.modelAnswer: The toy factory faced a strange problem after a new software update: the helper robots would not work correctly, with one robot repeating the same word and another refusing to pack a toy into its box. Ms. Huda studied the update's code line by line, and Dalia noticed that two commands had merged into one confusing word because a space was missing between them. Ms. Huda solved the problem by typing in the missing space, which let the robots understand the command again and return to sorting and packing.

keyWords.definition: a sequence of exact steps or instructions used to solve a problem or complete a task
keyWords.example: Engineers designed an algorithm to help the delivery robot choose the shortest route.

keyWords.definition: a failure of a machine or system to work correctly
keyWords.example: A sudden malfunction caused the elevator to stop between floors.

keyWords.definition: to figure out exactly what is causing a problem
keyWords.example: The mechanic took an hour to diagnose the strange noise in the engine.

keyWords.definition: to use a command or action that cancels or takes priority over another one
keyWords.example: The pilot had to override the autopilot when the storm began.

keyWords.definition: the exact rules for how symbols, words, or commands must be arranged in code or language
keyWords.example: A single syntax mistake can stop an entire program from running.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the central idea of the story?
options: A factory abandons every single one of its robots after they repeatedly malfunction without explanation, and sends the workers home for good
A visiting child's careful observation helps engineers diagnose a confusing factory-wide malfunction down to one tiny coding error
A factory redesigns its robotic workforce overnight without warning the people who work there
An engineer and a technician disagree loudly about how to run the factory, and the problem stays unsolved
questions.why: The story centers on Dalia's observation helping Ms. Huda trace the robots' strange, factory-wide malfunction to a single missing space in the code.

wrong.A: The factory repairs rather than abandons its robots.
wrong.C: No redesign of the robots occurs; only a coding bug is corrected.
wrong.D: No public disagreement between an engineer and technician occurs.

questions.stem: Based on the story, what is the most likely technical reason the robots freeze when given the merged command?
options: A syntax error merges two commands into one the robots cannot interpret
The robots' batteries drain faster after any update
A sensor malfunction prevents the robots from detecting nearby toys
The robots were never given any commands that morning at all
questions.why: Two commands accidentally merge into one unreadable word, a syntax problem the robots cannot correctly parse, so they freeze.

wrong.B: Battery drain is never mentioned as a cause.
wrong.C: A sensor problem is not what the story describes.
wrong.D: The robots do receive a command; they simply cannot interpret it.

questions.stem: In the story, the word diagnose most nearly means —
options: to replace a broken machine part with a new one
to shut a whole machine down completely
to figure out exactly what is causing a problem
to pack a box according to instructions
questions.why: Ms. Huda and Dalia work to diagnose the malfunction, meaning they are figuring out exactly what is causing the robots to freeze.

wrong.A: Replacing a part is a separate idea from diagnosing a problem.
wrong.B: Shutting a machine down is not the meaning of diagnose.
wrong.D: Packing a box is unrelated to diagnosing a malfunction.

questions.stem: What can be inferred about why Ms. Huda studies the update "line by line" rather than guessing at a fix?
options: She actually suspects the robots' hardware, not their software, is at fault, so she checks the machines
She genuinely wants to memorize the entire software update for later personal use at home
She is simply following strict factory rules that require a slow, careful review of all work
A single misplaced character can be nearly invisible unless each line is checked systematically
questions.why: Since the bug is just one missing space, careful line-by-line checking is necessary to catch something nearly impossible to notice otherwise.

wrong.A: The story places the fault in the software's syntax, not the hardware.
wrong.B: Memorizing the update for later is not mentioned.
wrong.C: No factory rule requiring a slow review is described.

questions.stem: Place these events in the order they occur in the story.
options: Ms. Huda fixes the bug, the update is installed, Dalia notices the merged words, the robots freeze
The update is installed, the robots freeze, Dalia notices the merged words, Ms. Huda fixes the bug
Dalia notices the merged words, the robots freeze, the update is installed, Ms. Huda fixes the bug
The robots freeze, Ms. Huda fixes the bug, the update is installed, Dalia notices the merged words
questions.why: The update is installed first, causing the robots to freeze; Dalia then spots the merged words, and Ms. Huda fixes the bug last.

wrong.A: The bug cannot be fixed before the update even causes a problem.
wrong.C: The update must be installed before the robots can freeze.
wrong.D: Freezing happens only after the update is installed, not before.

questions.stem: Why does the author most likely emphasize that the entire malfunction was caused by a single missing space?
options: To suggest that the update's engineers were careless and poorly trained
To show that Ms. Huda rewrote the whole update from scratch
To explain how factories generally schedule software updates
To highlight how an extremely small coding error can disrupt an entire system
questions.why: Emphasizing the tiny size of the error underscores how a minor oversight produced a factory-wide malfunction.

wrong.A: The story does not suggest the engineers were generally careless or poorly trained.
wrong.B: Ms. Huda corrects one small error rather than rewriting the update.
wrong.C: Scheduling practices are not addressed in the story.

questions.stem: Which comparison best matches the relationship between the robots' malfunction and its cause, as described in the story?
options: A malfunction is to a missing space as a locked door is to a missing key
A malfunction is to an entire factory as a toy is to a box in a shop
A malfunction is to Dalia as an update is to Ms. Huda and the class
A malfunction is to a technician as a joke is to a robot or a machine
questions.why: Just as a locked door cannot open without the correct key, the robots could not run correctly without the missing space in the code.

wrong.B: This pairs unrelated nouns rather than a cause and its effect.
wrong.C: This pairs people and things, not a cause-and-effect relationship.
wrong.D: This pairs unrelated ideas rather than cause and effect.

questions.stem: What does the story suggest would happen if Ms. Huda tried to override the frozen robots' behavior without first finding the bug?
options: The robots would immediately and start working perfectly again on their own without help
The robots would gradually develop a permanent personality change over time, like new people
The robots would likely keep malfunctioning, since the underlying syntax error would still be unresolved
The robots would flatly and permanently refuse to ever receive another software update from anyone
questions.why: Since the flaw lives in the merged command itself, simply overriding the robots' current behavior would not fix the underlying syntax error causing it.

wrong.A: The story shows the problem requires finding and fixing the actual bug, not that it resolves on its own.
wrong.B: Robots do not develop personalities in this story.
wrong.D: Nothing in the story suggests robots can refuse future updates.

HIGH.prompt: The poll says machines can misbehave but can never truly choose to disobey like a person can. Do you agree or disagree? Support your argument with evidence from the story about the robots' strange behavior.
checklist: I stated a clear position on the poll statement.
I supported my position with specific evidence from the story.
I addressed at least one point someone might make against my view.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I agree that machines can misbehave but never truly choose to disobey the way a person can. In the story, the robots freeze, repeat words, and refuse to pack toys, which looks exactly like a strike. However, the story makes clear that a single syntax error, a missing space that merged two commands into one unreadable word, is the actual cause, not any feeling of anger or rebellion. Someone might argue that the robots' refusal looks just like a person's refusal to work, but a person could choose to keep working despite frustration, while the robots had no such choice at all; they simply could not interpret a command that no longer made sense, and once Ms. Huda corrected that one tiny error, every robot cooperated again exactly as before.

LOW.stem: What job do the robots do at the factory?
options: They paint toys and ship them
They sort toys and pack boxes
They build toys from wood
They fix broken toys
LOW.why: In the text, the robots sort toys and pack boxes.

wrong.A: The robots do not paint or ship toys in the story.
wrong.C: The story never says the robots build toys.
wrong.D: The story never says the robots fix toys.

LOW.stem: In the story, what is an update?
options: A new toy for the box
A worker at the factory
A screen on the wall
New code for the robots
LOW.why: In the story, an update is new code for the robots.

wrong.A: An update is code, not a toy.
wrong.B: An update is not a person.
wrong.C: The screen shows the code, but it is not the update.

LOW.stem: Why does Dalia look very close at the screen?
options: She wants to find the problem
She wants to play a game
She is tired of the robots
She wants to call her mom
LOW.why: The robots are broken, so Dalia looks closely to find what is wrong with the code.

wrong.B: Nothing in the story says she plays a game.
wrong.C: She is trying to help, not leave the robots.
wrong.D: The story never mentions Dalia's mom.

LOW.stem: What happens right after Ms. Huda adds the space?
options: The workers go home
The robots keep standing still
The robots sort and pack again
The screen turns off
LOW.why: After she adds the space, the robots work again and sort and pack like before.

wrong.A: The workers do not go home in the story.
wrong.B: The robots stop standing still after the fix.
wrong.D: The story never says the screen turns off.

MID.stem: Who is Ms. Huda in the story?
options: Dalia's teacher at school
A worker who packs boxes
The factory's lead engineer
Dalia's aunt from home
MID.why: The text calls Ms. Huda the factory's lead engineer.

wrong.A: She works at the factory, not at Dalia's school.
wrong.B: She studies the code; she is not a box packer.
wrong.D: The story says Dalia's uncle is the engineer, not an aunt.

MID.stem: In the story, the word jumbled means —
options: mixed up and hard to read
quick and easy to follow
loud and very exciting
new and freshly made
MID.why: Two commands joined into one confusing word, so the command was mixed up and the robots could not read it.

wrong.B: A jumbled command is hard to follow, not easy.
wrong.C: The word is about confusion, not loud sound.
wrong.D: Jumbled does not mean new.

MID.stem: Why do the robots freeze in place?
options: Their wheels run out of power
The workers turn them all off
They get angry at the workers
They can not read the command
MID.why: The text says the robots can not understand a jumbled command like that, so they freeze.

wrong.A: Power is never mentioned as the problem.
wrong.B: The workers do not turn them off.
wrong.C: The story says robots can not really get angry.

MID.stem: Why does Dalia spot the bug when others have not?
options: She watches the screen very closely
She has fixed robots many times
She wrote the update last night
She is taller than the workers
MID.why: Dalia leans in and studies the screen with real curiosity, so her careful looking helps her see the missing space.

wrong.B: The story never says she has fixed robots before.
wrong.C: The workers installed the update, not Dalia.
wrong.D: Her height has nothing to do with the story.

HIGH.stem: According to the story, why did the technicians install the new update?
options: To make the robots work faster
To teach the robots a new word
To replace the old robots
To fix small old problems
HIGH.why: In the text, the update was meant to correct minor malfunctions left from the preceding version.

wrong.A: Speed is not given as the reason.
wrong.B: Teaching a new word is not the goal of the update.
wrong.C: The update replaces instructions, not the robots.

HIGH.stem: In the story, the word irregular most nearly means —
options: out of the ordinary
very easy to fix
carefully planned
common and expected
HIGH.why: Ms. Huda searches for anything irregular, meaning something unusual that could explain the malfunction.

wrong.B: Irregular does not describe how easy a fix is.
wrong.C: A planned thing is the opposite of what she hunts for.
wrong.D: Common things would not be a sign of trouble.

HIGH.stem: What does the technician's nervous laughter suggest?
options: He thinks the robots are broken forever
He is uneasy about the strange scene
He planned the problem as a prank
He is proud of the new update
HIGH.why: He laughs nervously at the bizarre scene, which shows he is uneasy and is using a joke to cope.

wrong.A: Nothing says he believes the damage is forever.
wrong.C: The story gives no sign of a prank.
wrong.D: A proud person would not laugh nervously at a failure.

HIGH.stem: How does the author mainly organize the story?
options: Two robots are compared side by side
A problem appears and then is solved
The events are told from last to first
A list of rules explains how robots work
HIGH.why: The story begins with the robots freezing, then Dalia and Ms. Huda find the cause and fix it.

wrong.A: The story does not compare two robots.
wrong.C: The events are told in the order they happen.
wrong.D: The story is a tale, not a list of rules.
